extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners / PR professionals pitching journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for PR pros on whether, when, and how to follow up with journalists after sending a media pitch, including timing, length, personalization, and channel advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing matters / wait 2–3 days
rubrics_metrics.description: 3 in 10 journalists want two to three days to look over a pitch before a PR pro follows up with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, consider the nature of the publication and the timeliness of the story. Almost half (49%) of journalists sometimes get a pitch they would like to cover but can’t due to time or resource constraints. Also consider time of day: worst times to follow up are before 8:00 a.m. and after 4:00 p.m.; the sweet spot is between 8:00 a.m. and noon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep it brief (100–300 words for pitches; follow-ups shorter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vast majority of journalists want media pitches that are brief and to the point; ideal length is between 100 and 300 words. Follow-up messages should be even shorter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quickly summarize your earlier pitch, remind the reporter why this story is newsworthy for their audience, and include any new updates. Mention your original email’s subject line to make it easier for the journalist to retrieve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use email as the primary channel
rubrics_metrics.description: Email remains the best avenue for pitching journalists — 96% prefer it over any other method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use email for both your original pitch and follow-up. Unless you’ve already built a rapport with the journalist on social, reconsider before switching channels or sliding into direct messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try a new angle if you don’t get a response
rubrics_metrics.description: If your original pitch didn’t get a response, consider reasons why and try a new, more compelling angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether timing, fit, or lack of originality were the issue. Journalists repeatedly note a need for more original stories and unique angles; avoid sending generic 'content' that lacks a fresh hook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit persistence — follow up once (at most)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most reporters (62%) advise following up once (and once only); fewer than 1 in 10 recommend more than one follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you’ve followed up and still haven’t gotten a reply, move on. The majority of journalists will block a media relations person who follows up persistently; one reporter rejected pitches because senders 'send too many ‘follow-up' emails or ask if I had a chance to review what they pitched.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsider your audience: relevance and prior coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Before following up, ensure the pitch is relevant to the journalist’s audience and circulation area and that you’re not pitching something they’ve already covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the journalist’s previous stories and coverage area. Personalize correctly by addressing them by name, referencing recent work, and explaining why your story fits their specific beats or audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalize correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization must be accurate and specific to the journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check the original email for personalization errors. Reference the reporter’s recent work, address them by name, and explain the specific fit for their coverage. Tools (e.g., AI pitch features) can help craft personalized copy, but ensure factual correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include new updates to increase newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are developments since your original pitch, include them in the follow-up to make the story more compelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly call out what’s new and why it changes the pitch’s relevance or timeliness; this can justify a follow-up and reignite interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention the original subject line for easy reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference your original email’s subject line in the follow-up to help journalists locate the prior message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear reference reduces friction for busy reporters and makes it easier for them to retrieve and reconsider your original pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play the long game — build relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejected or unpicked pitch can still be valuable as an opportunity to start building relationships with journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t assume a missed pickup means a bad pitch; breaking news, inbox volume, or schedules often prevent coverage. Follow-up etiquette and respectful persistence (within limits) help cultivate long-term media relationships.
